title: Agentic Code Review and Validation
text:
Technical setup
This section provides some step-by-step instructions on how to install relevant software discussed and presented throughout the course.

Download and install git
Git is a free and open source distributed version control system designed to handle everything from small to very large projects with speed and efficiency. It comes as a command line software, i.e., natively there is no graphical user interface (GUI) as you may be used to from other commonly used software. However, GUI applications (which make the handling of git commands easier, especially for beginners) are available and described in GitHub Desktop.

Step 1: Go to https://git-scm.com/downloads
Step 2: Download the git distribution for your specific operating system (Windows, MacOS, Linux) (see Figure 1)







Figure 1: Install git from the git website





GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop is a free, open-source application that provides a graphical user interface (GUI) for interacting with Git and GitHub, simplifying tasks like committing, pushing, and pulling changes, as well as managing repositories. It aims to make using Git and collaborating on GitHub more accessible, especially for those who prefer not to use the command line.

Step 1: Go to https://github.com/apps/desktop
Step 2: Click on Download now (see Figure 2)
Step 3: You will be prompted to the correct distribution for your specific operating system (Windows, MacOS, Linux)







Figure 2: Install the GitHub Desktop to interact with Git via a graphical user interface.





GitHub Account Setup
GitHub is a web-based platform that uses Git for version control and collaboration on software development projects. It allows developers to store, manage, and share code, making it easier to work together on projects and track changes. Think of it as a social coding platform and a cloud-based storage for code.
You can sign-up for a free account (which is more than sufficient enough for the purposes of this course), which gives you access to GitHub’s core features including:

Access to GitHub Copilot
Unlimited repositories (to collaborate on public and private projects)
Integrated code reviews
Automated workflows (via CI/CD integrations and GitHub Actions with 2,000CI/CD minutes per month)
Community support

Often larger organizations such as universities and companies also have (paid) enterprise accounts which give you access to even more features. To sign up for a GitHub account, follow these steps:

Step 1: Go to https://github.com
Step 2: Enter the E-mail address that should be associated with your GitHub account and press Sign up for GitHub (see Figure 3)
Step 3: Enter more details like your password to access GitHub, a username and your country and click Create account







Figure 3: Landing page to sign up for a GitHub account.





GitHub Copilot
GitHub Copilot is a generative AI tool that functions as a coding assistant to help you write code faster and so much more.

Step 1: Go to https://github.com/features/copilot
Step 2: Click on Get started for free. Be aware that there also also paid plans (e.g., Copilot Pro) and ensure that you sign up for the free plan, which is enough to get started and explore this tool.
Step 3: You can use GitHub Copilot directly via a chatbot on Github.com (e.g., to learn more about code in repositories or to ask questions on existing software tools that are hosted on GitHub) or in supported IDE (Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio, RStudio, JetBrains IDEs, Azure Data Studio, Xcode, Vim/Neovim, and Eclipse)




Signup landing website for GitHub Copilot.




Visual Studio (VS) Code
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is a free, open-source, and highly customizable code editor developed by Microsoft. It’s known for its lightweight nature, powerful features, and extensive extensibility through extensions. VS Code is used by developers for various tasks, including editing, debugging, and managing code. One of the key strengths of VS Code is its extensibility. The VS Code Marketplace offers a vast collection of extensions that add functionality for various programming languages, frameworks, and tools.

Step 1: Go to https://code.visualstudio.com
Step 2: The download button for your specific operating system (Windows, MacOS, Linux; see Figure 4)
Step 3: Follow the installation prompts that you will be guided through







Figure 4: Download and install the VSCode integrated development environment (IDE).





Fork the GitHub Codespaces Template
GitHub Codespaces provides cloud-powered development environments for any activity - whether it’s a long-term project, or a short-term task like reviewing a pull request. You can work with these environments from Visual Studio Code or in a browser-based editor. GitHub Codespaces comes with a free plan for personal accounts but can also be extended to a paid plan that comes with more storage and compute hours.
One of the core strengths is that it’s cloud-based and dependencies can be dockerized, i.e., it allows researchers to create and access complete and customized development environments remotely, directly from a web browser. For example, you may be using a specific combination of a local operating system (Windows, MacOS or Linux), a specific version of a programming language (e.g., R version 4.4.1) and a suite of R packages in their respective versions. With GitHub Codespaces you can create such a highly customized environments and reproduce (even share) these at the click of a button.
We created such an environment for this course and you can access it by following these steps:

Sign up for a (free) GitHub account (see GitHub Account Setup) and GitHub Copilot (GitHub Copilot)
Go to https://github.com/janickweberpals/codespaces-template
Click on Fork (Figure 5) to create a forked version on your GitHub account







Figure 5: Fork the codespace template.




Optional: Rename your forked version (e.g., my-codespace-ICPE25, see Figure 6)







Figure 6: Rename the personal fork (copy) of the codespace.




Go to Code > Codespaces > Create codespace on main (Figure 7)







Figure 7: Creating and starting a codespace on the main branch.

title: 2  Clinical Study Protocol
text:
8.1 Study design
Research design: New-user active-comparator cohort study.
Rationale for study design choice: The new-user active-comparator design addresses confounding by indication through judicious selection of a comparator group and subsequent statistical balancing of measured confounders via a propensity score. Restricting to new users avoids prevalent-user bias (depletion of susceptibles). The overlap (ATO) estimand is chosen because both treatment groups are represented throughout the propensity-score distribution, making equipoise-based comparison most meaningful.

title: 2  Clinical Study Protocol
text:
8.2 Study design diagram
The study window spans from a 365-day washout period before index date (time 0) through up to 365 days of follow-up. Baseline covariates are assessed in the window [–365, 0]; treatment is assigned at time 0 (first dispensing); the primary composite event or censoring occurs during [1, 365].

title: 2  Clinical Study Protocol

8.3 Setting

8.3.1 Context and rationale for definition of time 0
Time 0 is defined as the date of first dispensing of Drug A or Drug B for each patient. The new-user requirement is operationalized by a 12-month washout window with no prior dispensing of either drug.

title: 2  Clinical Study Protocol
text:
8.4 Variables

8.4.1 Context and rationale for exposure(s) of interest
Treatment group is assigned at time 0 via a logistic-regression-based propensity mechanism that embeds confounding by indication: Drug A (the newer agent) is preferentially initiated in younger patients with higher BMI and lower comorbidity burden. This mimics real-world prescribing behaviour and makes PS-based confounding adjustment necessary.
Algorithm to define duration of exposure effect: A 45-day grace period is applied. Informative censoring is modelled as exponential dropout with mean 400 days, representing disenrollment or treatment discontinuation.


Show the code
dplyr::tibble(
  `Exposure group`   = c("Drug A", "Drug B"),
  `R variable`       = c("`treatment = 1`; `treatment_label = 'Drug A'`",
                          "`treatment = 0`; `treatment_label = 'Drug B'`"),
  `Type of entry`    = c("Incident (new user)", "Incident (new user)"),
  `Washout window`   = c("[-365, -1]", "[-365, -1]"),
  `Grace period`     = c("45 days", "45 days")
) |>

8.4.2 Context and rationale for outcome(s) of interest
The primary outcome is the composite of all-cause mortality or hospitalization for heart failure, whichever occurs first. This is simulated using a Weibull proportional-hazards model (simsurv::simsurv) with a baseline scale calibrated to produce a 1-year cumulative incidence of approximately 3.4% in the Drug B arm, matching the published source study.

  `Primary?`         = c("Yes"),

  `R variable`       = c("`status` (1 = event, 0 = censored); `time` (follow-up days)"),
  `Washout window`   = c("N/A"),
  `Simulation model` = c("Weibull(lambda = 1.8e-5, gamma = 1.15); maxt = 365 days")
) |>

  gt_style()

8.4.3 Context and rationale for follow up
Follow-up begins 1 day after cohort entry (time 0) and ends at the earliest of: the primary composite event, informative censoring (dropout), or the administrative end of study at day 365. A 45-day grace period is allowed for treatment gaps.


Show the code

  `Rule`                           = c(

    "Primary composite event",
    "Informative censoring (dropout)",

  `Definition`                     = c(
    "Day 1 after cohort entry (time 0 + 1 day)",
    "First occurrence of HF hospitalization or all-cause mortality",
    "Exponential(rate = 1/400); models disenrollment or discontinuation within the 45-day grace period",
    "Day 365 (52 weeks)"
  ),
  `R implementation`               = c(
    "`time = min(event_time, cens_time, 365)`",
    "`status = 1` if event_time ≤ cens_time AND ≤ 365",
    "`cens_time ~ rexp(n, rate = 1/400)`",
    "`maxt = 365` in `simsurv::simsurv()`"
  )
) |>

  gt_style()

title: 2  Clinical Study Protocol
text:
8.5 Data analysis

8.5.1 Context and rationale for analysis plan
The estimand of interest is the average treatment effect in the overlap (ATO) population — patients for whom either treatment would realistically have been prescribed (clinical equipoise). This is achieved through propensity-score overlap weighting, which up-weights patients near the decision boundary and avoids the extrapolation problems of ATT or ATE weighting with extreme scores.

Show the code
# A. Primary
dplyr::tibble(
  Element = c(
    "Hypothesis",
    "Exposure contrast",
    "Outcome",
    "Analytic software",
    "Propensity score model",
    "Confounding adjustment",
    "Outcome model",
    "Standard errors",
    "Missing data",
    "Subgroup analyses"
  ),
  Specification = c(
    "Drug A is not meaningfully different from Drug B on the composite endpoint (non-inferiority).",
    "Drug A vs. Drug B (new users).",
    "Composite: all-cause mortality or HF hospitalization (time-to-event).",
    "R ≥ 4.5; packages: WeightIt, cobalt, gtsummary, survival, ggsurvfit (see Section 9).",
    "Logistic regression: `treatment ~ age + female + race + region + bmi + prior_hf_hosp + diuretic_use + nephropathy + neuropathy + retinopathy + foot_ulcer + insulin_use + pad + afib + cardiomyopathy + ckd + copd + depression + dementia + metformin + sulfonylurea + sglt2i + statin + anticoagulant + n_hospitalizations + n_ed_visits + n_distinct_meds + comorbidity_index`; implemented via `WeightIt::weightit(method = 'glm', estimand = 'ATO')`.",
    "Propensity-score overlap (ATO) weighting; balance assessed with SMDs and Love plot (cobalt).",
    "Weighted Cox PH: `survival::coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treatment_label, weights = ato_weight, robust = TRUE)`.",

title: 2  Clinical Study Protocol
text:
8.6 Data sources

8.6.1 Context and rationale for data sources
Reason for selection: Fully simulated data are used to enable reproducible teaching without the need for restricted real-world data access.
Strengths: The simulation is calibrated to approximate a published source study in terms of cohort size, confounding structure, event rates, and effect size. It is generated deterministically from a fixed seed (seed = 20260614).
Limitations: Simulated data cannot capture real-world complexities such as informative loss to follow-up correlated with covariates, measurement error, unmeasured confounders, or data source heterogeneity across claims databases.
Data source provenance: All data are generated in memory by generate_cohort() in mock-study/02_data_generation.R. Nothing is written to disk.

title: 3  Primary Endpoint Analysis
text:
3.1 Background
This document implements a primary endpoint analysis following the general design of a target trial emulation comparing new users of Drug A versus Drug B in a chronic disease setting. It uses entirely synthetic data and generic drug labels.
The primary outcome is a composite of hospitalization for heart failure (HF) or all-cause mortality, assessed over up to 52 weeks of follow-up. Because treatment is not randomized, initiators of the two drugs differ at baseline (confounding by indication). We address this with propensity-score overlap (ATO) weighting, then estimate the treatment effect with a weighted Cox proportional-hazards model.
Show the code
# Generate the simulated cohort in memory by sourcing the data-generation
# function (nothing is read from / written to disk). Resolve the script path
# whether rendered from the project root or from inside mock-study/.
gen_script <- c("02_data_generation.R", file.path("mock-study", "02_data_generation.R"))
source(gen_script[file.exists(gen_script)][1])
cohort <- generate_cohort()

# Confounders to adjust for (baseline covariates).
covariates <- c(
  "age", "female", "race", "region",
  "bmi", "prior_hf_hosp", "diuretic_use",
  "nephropathy", "neuropathy", "retinopathy", "foot_ulcer", "insulin_use",
  "pad", "afib", "cardiomyopathy", "ckd",
  "copd", "depression", "dementia",
  "metformin", "sulfonylurea", "sglt2i", "statin", "anticoagulant",
  "n_hospitalizations", "n_ed_visits", "n_distinct_meds", "comorbidity_index"
)

# Human-readable variable labels (used by gtsummary tables).
var_labels <- list(
  age = "Age, years", female = "Female sex", race = "Race", region = "Region",
  bmi = "Body mass index, kg/m²", prior_hf_hosp = "Prior HF hospitalization",
  diuretic_use = "Diuretic use", nephropathy = "Diabetic nephropathy",

text: Important: This is a mock study created exclusively to illustrate the capabilities of Claude Code for agentic code review and validation. Drug names have been replaced with placeholders (Drug A, Drug B). All data are fully simulated. No real-world clinical conclusions should be drawn from this analysis.

title: 3  Primary Endpoint Analysis
text:
3.2 Step 1 — Baseline characteristics (before weighting)
Several covariates show meaningful imbalance (|SMD| > 0.1), confirming confounding by indication: Drug A initiators are younger, have higher BMI, and carry a lower cardiovascular/comorbidity burden.

title: 3  Primary Endpoint Analysis
section: 3.3 Step 2 — Propensity score estimation and overlap (ATO) weighting
text:
3.3 Step 2 — Propensity score estimation and overlap (ATO) weighting
We estimate the propensity score (probability of receiving Drug A) with a logistic regression on all baseline covariates, then derive overlap (ATO) weights. Overlap weights emphasize patients with propensity scores in the region of clinical equipoise and yield exact mean balance on every covariate included in the model.


Show the code
ps_formula <- reformulate(covariates, response = "treatment")

W <- weightit(
  ps_formula,
  data      = cohort,
  method    = "glm",     # logistic-regression propensity score
  estimand  = "ATO"      # average treatment effect in the overlap population
)

cohort$ato_weight <- W$weights
W


A weightit object
 - method: "glm" (propensity score weighting with GLM)
 - number of obs.: 28100
 - sampling weights: none
 - treatment: 2-category
 - estimand: ATO
 - covariates: age, female, race, region, bmi, prior_hf_hosp, diuretic_use, nephropathy, neuropathy, retinopathy, foot_ulcer, insulin_use, pad, afib, cardiomyopathy, ckd, copd, depression, dementia, metformin, sulfonylurea, sglt2i, statin, anticoagulant, n_hospitalizations, n_ed_visits, n_distinct_meds, comorbidity_index

  var.order    = "unadjusted",
  drop.distance = TRUE,
  sample.names = c("Unweighted", "ATO weighted"),

section: 3.4 Step 3 — Primary endpoint analysis (weighted Cox model)
text:
3.4 Step 3 — Primary endpoint analysis (weighted Cox model)
The treatment effect on the composite endpoint is estimated with a Cox proportional-hazards model incorporating the overlap weights. Robust (sandwich) standard errors account for the weighting.


Show the code
cox_wt <- coxph(
  Surv(time, status) ~ treatment_label,
  data    = cohort,
  weights = cohort$ato_weight,
  robust  = TRUE
)

tbl_regression(cox_wt, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  modify_header(estimate ~ "**HR**") |>
  modify_caption(
    "**Table 2. Primary composite endpoint — ATO-weighted hazard ratio**"

title: 3  Primary Endpoint Analysis
text:
3.5 Step 4 — One-year cumulative incidence


Show the code
fit_wt <- survfit(
  Surv(time, status) ~ treatment_label,
  data    = cohort,
  weights = cohort$ato_weight
)

risk_1yr <- summary(fit_wt, times = 365)
risk_tbl <- data.frame(
  Group         = sub("treatment_label=", "", risk_1yr$strata),
  `1-year risk` = sprintf("%.1f%% (95%% CI, %.1f%%-%.1f%%)",
                          100 * (1 - risk_1yr$surv),
                          100 * (1 - risk_1yr$lower),
                          100 * (1 - risk_1yr$upper)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(risk_tbl, caption = "Table 3. ATO-weighted 1-year risk by arm")

Group
1-year risk




Drug B

Drug A

Show the code
survfit2(
  Surv(time, status) ~ treatment_label,
  data    = cohort,
  weights = cohort$ato_weight
) |>
  ggsurvfit(type = "risk", linewidth = 1) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 365)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 365, 90)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative incidence of HF hospitalization or all-cause mortality",
    x = "Days since treatment initiation",
    y = "Cumulative incidence"
  )










3.5.1 Interpretation
After propensity-score overlap weighting, the risk of the composite endpoint is not meaningfully different between Drug A and Drug B initiators, with a hazard ratio close to the published estimate of 0.86 and a confidence interval that crosses 1.0. The crude (unweighted) analysis would have overstated a Drug A benefit because of confounding by indication — illustrating why balancing the treatment groups is essential.

file_labels <- c(
  "test_data_generation.R"         = "Data generation",
  "test_primary_endpoint_analysis.R" = "Primary endpoint analysis",
  "test_protocol_adherence.R"      = "Protocol adherence"
)

list(
  "test_data_generation.R"           = res_data,
  "test_primary_endpoint_analysis.R" = res_primary,
  "test_protocol_adherence.R"        = res_protocol
) |>
  purrr::imap(function(df, file) {
    dplyr::summarise(
      df,
      Suite        = file_labels[[file]],
      Tests        = dplyr::n(),
      Expectations = sum(Expectations),
      Passed       = sum(Passed),
      Failed       = sum(Failed),
      Skipped      = sum(Skipped),
      `Time (s)`   = round(sum(`Time (s)`), 1),
      Status       = dplyr::if_else(
        sum(Failed) + sum(Error) == 0,
        "✔ All pass",
        glue::glue("✖ {sum(Failed)} failed")
      )
    )
  }) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Validation summary") |>
  cols_align(align = "left",   columns = c(Suite, Status)) |>
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(Tests, Expectations, Passed, Failed, Skipped, `Time (s)`)) |>
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#2e7d32", weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Status, rows = grepl("✔", Status))
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(color = "#c62828", weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Status, rows = grepl("✖", Status))
  ) |>
  grand_summary_rows(
    columns  = c(Tests, Expectations, Passed, Failed, Skipped),
    fns      = list(Total = ~sum(.)),
    fmt      = ~ fmt_integer(.)
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), data_row.padding = px(3))
